title: Early Coral Bleaching Confirmed in the Florida Keys as El Niño-Driven Marine Heat Builds
detail: On July 12, 2026, USGS coral scientist Dr. Lauren Toth documented and photographed pale and bleached starlet coral (Siderastrea siderea) and lobed star coral (Orbicella annularis) at Newfound Harbor, an inshore patch reef in the Lower Florida Keys — visible confirmation that bleaching-level heat stress had reached the Keys reef tract during what has been an exceptionally hot 2026 summer. NOAA Coral Reef Watch's satellite bleaching alert system showed Alert Level 1 conditions across most of coastal Florida, including the Keys, as El Niño conditions officially strengthened through the Northern Hemisphere summer following NOAA's confirmation of onset in early June. NOAA's four-month outlook flags high bleaching risk not only for Florida and the Caribbean but also much of the North Pacific, including Hawai'i, later in the season. The observations follow earlier-than-usual bleaching signs reported near PortMiami in late May 2026, when roughly 25% of surveyed corals showed early stress — months ahead of the historical July–October bleaching season — prompting University of Miami's Rescue a Reef program to accelerate transplanting of heat-tolerant 'super coral' genotypes. Florida's reef tract has already lost over 90% of its coral cover since the 1970s, and reef managers warn that a second consecutive bleaching season, on the heels of the fourth global mass bleaching event that impacted 84.4% of world reef area through 2025, would leave already-weakened colonies with little time to recover.

media.caption: Bleached coral confirmed at Newfound Harbor in the Lower Florida Keys as El Niño-driven heat stress builds, July 2026
